title: Poop Color After Drinking: Green, Yellow, Pale, or Black?
excerpt: Green or yellow poop after drinking is usually harmless and comes from food moving too fast. Here's what each color means, how long it lasts, and which colors need a doctor.
metaDescription: Green poop after drinking? Why alcohol changes stool color, what green, yellow, pale, black, and red mean, how long it lasts, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a strange poop color the day after drinking is usually harmless. Green or yellow stool most often means food moved through your gut too fast for bile to finish turning brown, which alcohol is good at causing. Food dyes in colorful drinks and mixers, dark beers, red wine, and hangover remedies like Pepto-Bismol can also change the color for a day or two. A few colors are different, though. **Black, tarry stool, red or maroon blood, and pale, clay-colored stool that keeps happening are not hangover symptoms** and need a doctor, sometimes urgently.

**The quick guide:** Green or yellow after a night out, with no other worrying symptoms, usually settles within a day or two once you eat normally and stop drinking. Black stool after Pepto-Bismol or iron pills is expected and harmless. Black and sticky like tar (without those), bright red or maroon blood, pale or white stool, or any odd color that lasts more than a few days needs medical attention.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** if you pass black, tarry stool or a lot of red or maroon blood, especially with dizziness, fainting, a racing heart, or vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds. **See a doctor soon** if your stool is pale, gray, or clay-colored more than once, particularly with dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, or pain in the upper right belly; if you see any blood in your stool; if diarrhea lasts more than two days or comes with a high fever or severe belly pain; or if an unusual color keeps coming back after you've stopped drinking. If someone is confused, can't stay awake, or is vomiting and can't keep anything down after heavy drinking, treat it as possible alcohol poisoning and get help now.

## Why Poop Is Brown in the First Place

To understand why poop changes color after drinking, it helps to know why it's normally brown.

Your liver makes **bile**, a yellow-green fluid that helps you digest fat. Bile is stored in the gallbladder and squeezed into your small intestine after you eat. Bile gets its color from pigments, mainly **bilirubin**, which comes from the normal breakdown of old red blood cells.

As food and bile travel through your intestines, gut bacteria slowly change those pigments. Bilirubin is converted step by step into compounds that are brown. By the time stool reaches the end of your colon, the usual result is that familiar brown color.

That means two things control poop color:

1. **How much bile reaches the gut.** Less bile means paler stool.
2. **How long stool spends in the gut.** Less time means the green and yellow pigments don't fully turn brown.

Alcohol can affect both of these, which is why the morning after can bring some surprises. What you ate and drank, and any medicines you took, can add a third layer on top.

## Green Poop After Drinking

Green is the color people search for most, and it's usually the least worrying.

### Reason 1: Food moved through too fast

Alcohol speeds up the movement of your gut and irritates its lining. It also makes the intestines less able to absorb water. The result is looser stool that rushes through, often called the "beer poops" or hangover diarrhea. When things move that fast, the green bile pigments don't have time to be turned brown by your gut bacteria, so the stool comes out green.

This is the same reason anyone with a stomach bug or a bout of diarrhea can see green stool. It's a sign of speed, not of damage. Once your gut slows down again, color goes back to normal, usually within a day or two. If loose stools are your main problem, our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains the causes and what helps.

### Reason 2: Green drinks and food dyes

Many party drinks get their color from artificial dyes. Blue and green dyes (in blue curaçao cocktails, colored shots, sports drinks, energy drinks, and the green beer that shows up around St. Patrick's Day) can pass through your gut partly unabsorbed and tint your stool green, teal, or even a blue-green that looks alarming. Purple and blue dyes can also mix with the natural yellow-brown to produce green.

If you remember drinking something brightly colored, that's very likely the explanation. Dye-related color changes typically clear within a day or two once the drink is out of your system.

### Reason 3: What you ate before or after

Late-night food matters too. Leafy greens, green-frosted cakes, and some candies can turn stool green. So can iron supplements in some people, although iron more often makes stool dark green or black.

### When green poop is worth checking

Green stool by itself is rarely a concern. It's worth seeing a doctor if green, watery diarrhea goes on for more than a couple of days, if it comes with a fever or severe cramping, or if you've recently taken antibiotics and now have frequent, watery, foul-smelling diarrhea. Those can point to an infection rather than a hangover.

## Yellow Poop After Drinking

Yellow stool has some of the same causes as green.

**Fast transit.** Bile starts out more yellow, so stool that rushes through can look yellow or yellow-green instead of brown. This is common during hangover diarrhea and usually fades within a day or two.

**Fatty food.** A greasy late-night meal (fries, pizza, burgers, kebabs) can leave stool lighter, softer, and more yellow, especially if your gut is already irritated and moving fast.

**Yellow, greasy, floating stool that keeps happening.** This one is different. Stool that is pale yellow, shiny or oily, unusually foul-smelling, floats, and is hard to flush can be a sign that you're not absorbing fat properly. One possible cause is a problem with the pancreas, which makes the enzymes that digest fat. Heavy drinking over a long period is one of the leading causes of chronic pancreatitis (long-term inflammation of the pancreas). Other causes include gallbladder and bile duct problems, celiac disease, and gut infections such as giardia.

A single yellowish stool after a big night is not a reason to panic. Greasy, floating stools that keep showing up over weeks, especially with weight loss or upper belly pain that spreads to your back, are a reason to book an appointment.

## Pale, Gray, or Clay-Colored Poop

Pale stool is the color change that deserves the most attention, because it can mean bile isn't reaching your gut.

Remember that bile is what gives stool its color. If stool turns pale, gray, white, or the color of putty or clay, it can mean the flow of bile is blocked or reduced. Possible causes include:

- **Liver inflammation**, including alcohol-related hepatitis, which can develop in people who drink heavily over time
- **Gallstones** blocking the bile duct
- **Pancreas problems**, including inflammation or, rarely, a growth pressing on the bile duct
- **Some medicines**, and barium from certain X-ray tests (barium can make stool look white for a few days, which is expected)

Pale stool from a blocked bile flow often comes with other signs, because the bile pigment that can't get out through the gut backs up into your blood instead:

- **Dark urine**, like tea or cola, even when you're drinking water
- **Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes** (jaundice)
- **Itchy skin**
- **Pain in the upper right belly**, under the ribs
- Fever, nausea, or feeling generally unwell

Dark urine on its own the morning after drinking is usually just dehydration, and it lightens once you drink water. The combination of pale stool and dark urine that stays dark despite water is the pattern to take seriously. If you notice pale stool more than once, or pale stool together with any of the signs above, see a doctor promptly. If you also have a high fever, severe belly pain, or confusion, go to urgent care or the emergency room.

## Black Poop After Drinking

Black stool has harmless causes and serious ones, so it's worth slowing down here.

### Harmless causes of black stool

- **Pepto-Bismol and other bismuth products.** This is the most common reason people see black stool after a night out. Bismuth subsalicylate, the active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol and similar pink stomach remedies, reacts with small amounts of sulfur in your gut and turns stool (and sometimes your tongue) black. The product labels mention this. It's harmless and goes away a few days after you stop taking it.
- **Iron supplements**, including multivitamins with iron, often make stool very dark green or black.
- **Dark foods and drinks.** Black licorice, blueberries, and very dark foods can darken stool. Dark beers and red wine can contribute too, though they're less likely to turn stool truly black on their own.

### When black stool is an emergency

Black stool caused by bleeding looks and behaves differently. Doctors call it **melena**. It is:

- Jet black, sticky, and shiny, like tar
- Often with a strong, unusually foul smell
- Sometimes with dizziness, weakness, paleness, shortness of breath, or a fast heartbeat

Melena usually means bleeding high in the digestive tract, such as the stomach, upper small intestine, or esophagus (the tube from your mouth to your stomach). By the time the blood reaches the end of the gut, it has been digested and turned black. Alcohol is relevant here in several ways:

- **Gastritis and ulcers.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and combining it with anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin raises the risk of stomach bleeding. That's why those painkillers carry a label warning about stomach bleeding for people who have three or more drinks a day.
- **Tears from forceful vomiting.** Hard, repeated vomiting after drinking can tear the lining where the esophagus meets the stomach (a Mallory-Weiss tear). Most are small and heal on their own, but some bleed.
- **Swollen veins in the esophagus.** In people with advanced alcohol-related liver disease, enlarged veins in the esophagus (varices) can bleed heavily. This is a medical emergency.

If you have black, tarry stool and haven't taken bismuth or iron, get medical care the same day. If it comes with dizziness, fainting, a racing heart, or vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, call 911 or go to the emergency room. Don't wait to see if it passes.

If you're not sure whether Pepto-Bismol explains it, tell the doctor what you took. A simple stool test can check for blood. Our guide to [black stool after drinking](/never-hungover/black-stool-after-drinking) goes through how to tell Pepto-black from bleeding, and when bright red blood is more likely to be a hemorrhoid.

## Red or Maroon Poop After Drinking

Red stool also has a harmless side and a serious side.

**Red from food and drinks.** Red food dyes in fruit punch, colored mixers, gelatin shots, and some candies can tint stool red. Beets famously do it too, often along with pink urine. Cranberry juice and very large amounts of tomato products occasionally do. If the red color matches something you consumed and goes away within a day or two, food is the likely cause.

**Red from blood.** Bright red blood on the toilet paper or streaked on the outside of stool most often comes from hemorrhoids or a small tear near the anus (an anal fissure). Repeated hangover diarrhea and straining can irritate both. This kind of bleeding is common and usually minor, but it's still worth mentioning to a doctor, because the same sign can occasionally come from something more serious.

**Maroon or dark red stool, or a lot of blood,** can mean bleeding higher in the colon or a fast bleed from higher up. Heavy rectal bleeding, blood clots, or any bleeding with dizziness, weakness, or a fast heartbeat is an emergency.

A practical rule: if you haven't had beets or red-dyed drinks and you see red in or on your stool, treat it as blood until a doctor tells you otherwise.

## Orange Poop After Drinking

Orange stool is almost always about food or drink. Orange and red dyes in sports drinks, sodas, and cocktail mixers, along with foods rich in beta-carotene like carrots and sweet potatoes, are the usual reasons. Fast transit can also leave stool a lighter orange-yellow shade. If it settles within a day or two, it isn't a concern.

## Poop Color Cheat Sheet

| Color | Most likely reason after drinking | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Green | Fast transit (bile didn't turn brown); green or blue dyes; leafy greens | Usually clears in 1 to 2 days. See a doctor if diarrhea lasts more than 2 days or comes with fever. |
| Yellow | Fast transit; greasy food | Usually clears in 1 to 2 days. See a doctor if greasy, floating stools keep happening. |
| Pale, gray, clay, white | Reduced bile flow (liver, gallbladder, pancreas); barium | See a doctor soon, especially with dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, or upper right belly pain. |
| Black, not sticky | Pepto-Bismol, iron pills, dark foods | Expected if you took bismuth or iron. Ask a doctor if unsure. |
| Black and tarry | Bleeding in the upper digestive tract | Get medical care the same day. Emergency if dizzy, faint, or vomiting blood. |
| Red or maroon | Red dyes or beets, or bleeding | If no red food or drink explains it, see a doctor. Emergency if heavy or with dizziness. |
| Orange | Dyes, carrots, sweet potatoes | Usually harmless. |

## Why Alcohol Upsets Your Gut So Much

The color change is usually just a visible side effect of how alcohol affects your digestive system. A few things happen at once:

- **Faster movement.** Alcohol can speed up the muscle contractions that push food through your intestines, so there's less time to absorb water and less time for bile to turn brown.
- **Irritated lining.** Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach and intestines, which can cause inflammation, cramping, and looser stool.
- **Less water absorbed.** Alcohol interferes with how your gut absorbs water and salts, which adds to diarrhea and dehydration. Our guide on whether [alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains how that works.
- **Sugar and carbs.** Sugary mixers and large amounts of beer bring sugars and carbohydrates that can draw water into the gut or ferment, adding gas and loose stool.
- **Changes in gut bacteria.** Heavy drinking can disrupt the balance of gut bacteria, and those bacteria are part of what turns stool brown. You can read more in our article on [how alcohol affects your gut microbiome](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-affects-your-gut-microbiome-the-hidden-health-impact-2025).
- **Late-night food.** Greasy, spicy, or dyed foods eaten after drinking add their own effects.

Different drinks hit people differently. Some people notice beer causes the most trouble, likely from the volume of liquid and carbohydrates. Others react most to wine or sugary cocktails. If you see the same pattern every time with one type of drink, that's useful information.

## How Long Does It Last?

For a normal night out, color changes from fast transit or dyes usually clear within one to three days once you're eating normal meals and have stopped drinking. Your gut needs a bit of time to settle, and the colored food or drink needs to work its way out.

If an unusual color lasts longer than that, keeps coming back, or appears even when you haven't been drinking, it's worth having a doctor take a look. The same goes for any change that comes with other symptoms like weight loss, ongoing belly pain, or fatigue.

## What Helps Your Gut Settle

Most of what helps is simple:

- **Drink water and electrolytes.** Diarrhea and alcohol both pull fluids and salts from your body. Water plus an electrolyte drink or oral rehydration solution helps you recover. Sip steadily rather than gulping large amounts at once.
- **Eat bland, easy food.** Toast, rice, bananas, crackers, oatmeal, eggs, and broth are gentle on an irritated gut. Our list of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) has more ideas.
- **Skip the greasy, spicy, and sugary food for a day.** These can keep stool loose and colors odd.
- **Take a break from alcohol** for at least a day or two so your gut lining can recover. "Hair of the dog" just delays it.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** If you need one, ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can further irritate a stomach that's already inflamed from alcohol. Take any painkiller with food and stick to the label.
- **Know what Pepto-Bismol does.** It can help with an upset stomach and diarrhea, but expect black stool and possibly a dark tongue for a few days. It contains a salicylate, an aspirin-related compound, so check with a pharmacist if you take blood thinners, are allergic to aspirin, or are giving it to anyone under 18.
- **Probiotics are optional.** Some people try them to support gut bacteria after drinking. The evidence is mixed, and there is no good evidence that they prevent hangover diarrhea. Our article on [probiotics and alcohol](/never-hungover/probiotics-and-alcohol) covers what's known.

## How to Make It Less Likely Next Time

You can't control everything about how your gut reacts, but a few habits help:

- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed and cushions the gut lining.
- **Pace yourself.** About one standard drink per hour, with water in between, is easier on your whole system.
- **Watch the mixers.** Sugary, brightly dyed mixers add gut upset and strange colors. Soda water or plain mixers are gentler.
- **Notice your triggers.** If a particular drink reliably leads to diarrhea or green stool the next day, that's a signal to cut back on it.
- **Drink less overall.** Fewer drinks means less irritation, less dehydration, and fewer surprises in the bathroom.

## When a Color Change Isn't About Last Night

For most social drinkers, a strange poop color is a one-off that fades. But a few patterns suggest something more than a rough night, and they're worth saying plainly.

If you drink most days and you notice pale stools, dark urine, yellowing skin or eyes, swelling in your belly or legs, easy bruising, or black, tarry stools, those can be signs of alcohol-related liver disease or bleeding in the digestive tract. These need a doctor, not a home remedy. Being honest with the doctor about how much you drink helps them find the cause faster, and it's routine information for them to ask about.

If you're vomiting repeatedly after a night of heavy drinking, or vomiting blood, see our guide to [throwing up bile after drinking](/never-hungover/throwing-up-bile-after-drinking) for which signs mean you need care. Signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, slow or irregular breathing, being unable to stay awake, or seizures, need a 911 call right away. Our page on [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) lists them.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take before or during drinking. Research on DHM, mostly in animals with limited human data, suggests it may support alcohol metabolism and help protect the liver. There is no good evidence that DHM changes stool color, prevents hangover diarrhea, or treats any of the warning signs above, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

If you're interested in trying it as part of a more careful approach to drinking, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people typically use it. The basics still matter most: eat first, pace yourself, drink water, and see a doctor for any of the warning colors.

## The Bottom Line

Green or yellow poop after drinking is usually your gut moving too fast for bile to turn brown, sometimes helped along by dyed drinks or late-night food. It typically clears within a day or two. Black stool after Pepto-Bismol or iron is expected. But black, tarry stool, red or maroon blood you can't explain with food, and pale or clay-colored stool, especially with dark urine or yellow eyes, are not normal hangover signs. Those need a doctor, and black tarry stool or heavy bleeding with dizziness needs emergency care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why is my poop green after drinking alcohol?**

The most common reason is that alcohol speeds up your gut, so food and bile move through too fast for gut bacteria to turn the green-yellow bile pigments brown. Green or blue dyes in cocktails, shots, sports drinks, and green beer can also tint stool green, as can leafy greens. Green stool after a night out usually returns to normal within a day or two. See a doctor if green diarrhea lasts more than two days or comes with fever or severe cramps.

**Is yellow poop after drinking normal?**

Usually, yes. Yellow stool after drinking most often comes from fast transit or a greasy late-night meal, and it settles within a day or two. If you keep having pale yellow, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float and are hard to flush, that can mean you're not absorbing fat well, which can be linked to pancreas, gallbladder, or liver problems. That pattern is worth seeing a doctor about, especially if you drink heavily.

**Is pale or clay-colored poop after drinking dangerous?**

It can be. Pale, gray, white, or clay-colored stool can mean bile isn't reaching your gut, which can happen with liver inflammation (including alcohol-related hepatitis), gallstones, or pancreas problems. See a doctor promptly if it happens more than once, or right away if it comes with dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, upper right belly pain, or fever. The exception is barium from an X-ray test, which can make stool white for a few days.

**Why is my poop black after drinking?**

If you took Pepto-Bismol or another bismuth product, or iron pills, black stool is an expected and harmless side effect. Black, sticky, tar-like stool that you can't explain that way can mean bleeding in the stomach or upper digestive tract, which alcohol can contribute to through gastritis, ulcers, or tears from forceful vomiting. Get medical care the same day, and call 911 if you also feel dizzy, faint, or have vomited blood or coffee-ground-like material.

**Can red wine or beer change your poop color?**

They can contribute. Dark beers and red wine may make stool darker, and dyed mixers or red drinks can tint it red. More often, the color change after drinking comes from alcohol speeding up your gut rather than from the drink's own color. If you see red in your stool and haven't had beets or red-dyed food or drinks, treat it as possible blood and check with a doctor.

**How long does green poop last after drinking?**

Usually one to three days. Once you stop drinking, eat normal meals, and your gut slows down, bile has time to turn brown again. Dye-related colors also clear as the drink works its way out. If the color lasts longer, keeps coming back, or appears when you haven't been drinking, see a doctor.

**When should I worry about my poop color after drinking?**

Get help if you see black, tarry stool not explained by Pepto-Bismol or iron; red or maroon blood not explained by food; pale or clay-colored stool, especially with dark urine or yellow skin or eyes; diarrhea lasting more than two days; or any color change with dizziness, fainting, severe belly pain, high fever, or vomiting blood. Heavy bleeding or black stool with dizziness is an emergency, so call 911.

**Does DHM prevent green poop or diarrhea after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents green poop, diarrhea, or other gut symptoms after drinking. DHM has research suggesting it may support alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. Eating before drinking, pacing yourself, choosing gentler mixers, and drinking less are the more reliable ways to protect your gut.
